tier_reason: The README chart compares against BoringSSL AES-128/256-GCM. The harness is public (benches/benchmark.rs, BoringSSL behind --features boring), the build is stated (CC="clang -O3 -march=native"; build.rs forces clang at -O3), and the CPUs are AMD Zen 4 (microarchitecture only) and Apple M1. That would be tier A, but the record duplicates libaegis.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 16 KB encryption. AMD Zen 4, turbo off: AEGIS-128L 208.44 Gb/s vs BoringSSL AES-128-GCM 50.83 (~4.1x) and AES-256-GCM 47.68 (~4.4x); AEGIS-128X4 521.36 (~10.3x vs AES-128-GCM, ~10.9x vs AES-256-GCM); AEGIS-256 125.28 vs AES-256-GCM 47.68 (~2.6x). Apple M1: AEGIS-128L 114.61 vs BoringSSL AES-128-GCM 49.22 (~2.3x); AEGIS-128X2 134.05 (~2.7x); AEGIS-256 63.72 vs AES-256-GCM 41.6 (~1.5x). Ratios derived from page data.
corrections.hardware: AMD Zen 4 with turbo boost disabled (exact CPU model not stated); Apple M1 (MacBook Pro)
corrections.caveats: This is libaegis in another form. By default build.rs compiles the bundled libaegis C sources (git submodule src/c/libaegis -> jedisct1/libaegis, now aegis-aead/libaegis), and the Rust code is only FFI wrappers. The optional `pure-rust` feature is a separate, slower implementation and is not what the charts measure. The chart PNG is byte-identical to the one in the libaegis README, and both were last updated 2024-11-05, so the numbers are nearly two years old. The numbers are printed labels on the chart bars. The baseline is BoringSSL, not OpenSSL. On M1, AEGIS-128X4 (97.68) is slower than AEGIS-128L (114.61).

notes: Reject as a duplicate of aegis-aead/libaegis, which the catalogue already lists. rust-aegis is Rust bindings that bundle and compile libaegis's C code by default. It also has an independent pure-Rust backend, but that backend is slower and is not benchmarked. The numbers are not its own: the README chart is byte-identical (SHA-1 a76fffb3) to the libaegis README chart, which libaegis says is 'derived from libaegis'. The chart's Rust-crate labels suggest rust-aegis's cargo bench produced it, but it still measures the libaegis C code, and libaegis's catalogue entry already cites the same 208 vs 47.7 Gb/s figure.

tier_reason: The README Performance table matches perf/bench_results.json and perf/openssl.csv; for example, at 16 B it is 126.3 vs 396.4 ns (3.1x), and at 1 MiB it ties at 1.0x. The benchmark code is public (benches/aead.rs, and perf/openssl_bench.c built with cc -O2). The page states rustc 1.100-nightly, cargo bench with codegen-units=1, and an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.100-nightly; cargo bench --bench aead (Criterion; bench profile codegen-units=1; runtime SIMD dispatch, no target-cpu flag). OpenSSL 4.1.0-dev static build with runtime auto-dispatch (AVX-512 ChaCha and AVX-512 IFMA Poly1305 on this CPU). The OpenSSL driver perf/openssl_bench.c is built with cc -O2. aws-lc-rs 1.18 is benchmarked in the same Criterion harness.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 0 stars (GitHub repo created 2026-08-26; crate first published 2026-08-27); 108 crates.io downloads (v0.3.1)
corrections.caveats: A very new project (Aug 2026) with no independent verification. The README says it was developed with AI assistance and has not had a security audit. The OpenSSL comparison uses an OpenSSL 4.1.0-dev pre-release, and the setups are asymmetric: the C driver calls EVP_EncryptInit_ex with the cipher and key on every iteration, while the Rust cipher is keyed once outside the loop. That likely inflates the 2-3x gap at 16-256 B. At >=64 KiB it merely ties OpenSSL. Against aws-lc-rs it is slower at tiny sizes (0.8-0.9x) and about even at 512 B-1 KiB. It wins only at >=4 KiB (1.2-1.4x).

notes: The claimed ratios match the README table and the raw bench data. The license really is MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml, README and both LICENSE files), even though GitHub's detector reports only Apache-2.0.

tier_reason: docs/benchmarks.md has tables against ring and RustCrypto aes-gcm, with the exact reproduction commands. The Criterion benchmark code is public (benches/aes_gcm.rs). The page states rustc 1.96.0, a default release build plus the stated RUSTFLAGS cfg variant, and an Apple M4 Max.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Allocation-free encrypt beats ring at every size from 16 B to 16 KiB: 26.8 vs 57.8 ns at 16 B, 130.5 vs 216.6 ns at 1 KiB, and 1.77 vs 2.38 us at 16 KiB (8.64 vs 6.41 GiB/s). Decrypt also wins: 1.79 vs 2.19 us at 16 KiB. Against a default-build RustCrypto aes-gcm 0.10 it is 14x-43x faster. Against RustCrypto with its ARMv8 cfgs it is 3.4x-5.0x faster at >=256 B, but only ~1.3x-1.7x at 16-64 B. ring's key setup is faster (86 vs 94 ns).
corrections.caveats: This is a single-run laptop benchmark. The author states +/-10% run-to-run variance at sub-microsecond sizes and says to read results as 'tie/win/lose, not exact ratios' and to re-run on target Linux x86_64 hardware before integration decisions; no x86_64 numbers are published. The 14x-43x figure is against a RustCrypto build whose hardware AES is off by default on aarch64. It is not a GitHub fork, but per its NOTICE it vendors and adapts hasenbanck/rand_aes 0.7.0 (AES) and RustCrypto ghash/polyval backends. OpenSSL is used only for interop tests, not benchmarks. Only AES-256 is supported. The project has only 1 GitHub star.

notes: The numbers match docs/benchmarks.md. The record overstated the win over RustCrypto's ARMv8 build: 3.4-5.0x holds only from 256 B up. The main claim against ring (BoringSSL-derived) is accurate.
